primary_claim: A toy transformer retains provably predictively-defunct belief-state information (about a stochastic 'coin' that becomes irrelevant) in its residual stream rather than pruning it as optimal-prediction theory would suggest, and under sufficient capacity pressure from narrowing the residual stream, it sheds the oldest defunct information first, rather than the least predictively significant.

effect.metric: decodability of defunct 'coin' information from the residual stream after it becomes predictively irrelevant
effect.value: stays near 100% well after becoming predictively irrelevant, across divergence horizons and seeds

contradicts_or_qualifies: the initial hypothesis derived from optimal-prediction theory -- that a transformer should prune predictively irrelevant information -- was disproved; the model instead retains predictively defunct information in its residual stream long after it becomes irrelevant, indicating optimal prediction does not imply representational minimality
stated_future_work: use a state-space model where the state cannot be re-read by the attention layer, forcing the transformer to use memory to retain (or not) information about the coin, to more cleanly separate optimal prediction from representational minimality
limitations_stated: narrowing the residual stream alone did not serve as a true memory bottleneck, likely because the attention layer can re-derive the coin information from the context window
quote: This information is shed only when there is a sufficient amount of imposed capacity pressure, in which case the oldest predictively defunct information is shed first.
